• means that the sum of the infinite series properly <color=#3366CC>diverges</color> to infinity, in the sense that the partial sums increase
without bound.
In addition to defining a limit, infinity can be also used as a value in the extended real number system. Points labeled
and can be added to the <color=#3366CC>topological space</color> of the real numbers, producing the two-point compactification of the real
numbers. Adding algebraic properties to this gives us the <color=#3366CC>extended real numbers</color>. We can also treat and as the same,
leading to the one-point compactification of the real numbers, which is the real projective line. <color=#3366CC>Projective geometry</color> also
refers to a line at infinity in plane geometry, a plane at infinity in three-dimensional space, and a hyperplane at infinity
for general <color=#3366CC>dimensions</color>, each consisting of points at infinity.
Complex analysis
In <color=#3366CC>complex analysis</color> the symbol, called "infinity", denotes an unsigned infinite <color=#3366CC>limit</color>. The expression means that the
magnitude of grows beyond any assigned value. A point labeled can be added to the complex plane as a <color=#3366CC>topological</color>
<color=#3366CC>space</color> giving the one-point compactification of the complex plane. When this is done, the resulting space is a
one-dimensional complex manifold, or <color=#3366CC>Riemann surface</color>, called the extended complex plane or the <color=#3366CC>Riemann sphere</color>.
Arithmetic operations similar to those given above for the extended real numbers can also be defined, though there is
no distinction in the signs (which leads to the one exception that infinity cannot be added to itself). On the other hand,
this kind of infinity enables <color=#3366CC>division by zero</color>, namely for any nonzero <color=#3366CC>complex number</color>. In this context, it is often useful
to consider meromorphic functions as maps into the Riemann sphere taking the value of at the poles. The domain of a
complex-valued function may be extended to include the point at infinity as well. One important example of such
functions is the group of Möbius transformations (see Möbius transformation § Overview).
Nonstandard analysis
The original formulation of <color=#3366CC>infinitesimal calculus</color> by <color=#3366CC>Isaac Newton</color> and Gottfried Leibniz used infinitesimal quantities. In
the second half of the 20th century, it was shown that this treatment could be put on a rigorous footing through various
logical systems, including smooth infinitesimal analysis and nonstandard analysis. In the latter, infinitesimals are
invertible, and their inverses are infinite numbers. The infinities in this sense are part of a hyperreal field; there is no
equivalence between them as with the Cantorian <color=#3366CC>transfinites</color>. For example, if H is an infinite number in this sense, then
H + H = 2H and H + 1 are distinct infinite numbers. This approach to non-standard calculus is fully developed in Keisler
Set theory
A different form of "infinity" is the <color=#3366CC>ordinal</color> and <color=#3366CC>cardinal</color> infinities of set theory—a system of <color=#3366CC>transfinite numbers</color> first
developed by <color=#3366CC>Georg Cantor</color>. In this system, the first transfinite cardinal is <color=#3366CC>aleph-null</color> (0), the cardinality of the set of
<color=#3366CC>natural numbers</color>. This modern mathematical conception of the quantitative infinite developed in the late 19th century
from works by Cantor, <color=#3366CC>Gottlob Frege</color>, <color=#3366CC>Richard Dedekind</color> and others—using the idea of collections or sets.
Dedekind's approach was essentially to adopt the idea of <color=#3366CC>one-to-one correspondence</color> as a standard for comparing the
size of sets, and to reject the view of <color=#3366CC>Galileo</color> (derived from <color=#3366CC>Euclid</color>) that the whole cannot be the same size as the part.
(However, see Galileo's paradox where Galileo concludes that positive integers cannot be compared to the subset of
positive square integers since both are infinite sets.) An infinite set can simply be defined as one having the same size
as at least one of its <color=#3366CC>proper subsets</color> (a strictly smaller subset); this notion of infinity is called Dedekind infinite. The
diagram to the right gives an example: viewing lines as infinite sets of points, the left half of the lower blue line can be
mapped in a one-to-one manner (green correspondences) to the higher blue line, and, in turn, to the whole lower blue
line (red correspondences); therefore the whole lower blue line and its left half have the same cardinality, i.e. "size".
Cantor defined two kinds of infinite numbers: <color=#3366CC>ordinal numbers</color> and <color=#3366CC>cardinal numbers</color>. Ordinal numbers characterize
<color=#3366CC>well-ordered</color> sets, or counting carried on to any stopping point, including points after an infinite number have already
been counted. Generalizing finite and (ordinary) infinite <color=#3366CC>sequences</color> which are maps from the positive <color=#3366CC>integers</color> leads to
<color=#3366CC>mappings</color> from ordinal numbers to transfinite sequences. Cardinal numbers define the size of sets, meaning how many
members they contain, and can be standardized by choosing the first ordinal number of a certain size to represent the
cardinal number of that size. The smallest ordinal infinity is that of the positive integers, and any set which has the
cardinality of the integers is countably infinite.
If a set is too large to be put in one-to-one correspondence with the positive integers, it is called uncountable. <color=#3366CC>Cantor's</color>
<color=#3366CC>theorem</color> further proved that no largest cardinal exists, meaning that for every infinite set, there exists a larger set.
Cantor proclaimed that the collection of all sets had an unincreasable absolute infinity, which he identified with God.
Although initially controversial, Cantor's views prevailed and modern mathematics accepts actual infinity as part of a
consistent and coherent theory.
The theory of ordinal and cardinal numbers has been further developed since Cantor, with large countable ordinals and
<color=#3366CC>large cardinals</color> currently being studied in <color=#3366CC>mathematical logic</color>.
Cardinality of the continuum
One of Cantor's most important results was that the cardinality of the continuum is greater than that of the natural
numbers; that is, there are more real numbers R than natural numbers N. Namely, Cantor showed that.
The <color=#3366CC>continuum hypothesis</color> states that there is no <color=#3366CC>cardinal number</color> between the cardinality of the reals and the
cardinality of the natural numbers, that is,.This hypothesis cannot be proved or disproved within the widely accepted
<color=#3366CC>Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory</color>, even assuming the <color=#3366CC>Axiom of Choice</color>.
<color=#3366CC>Cardinal arithmetic</color> can be used to show not only that the number of points in a <color=#3366CC>real number line</color> is equal to the number
of points in any segment of that line, but also that this is equal to the number of points on a plane and, indeed, in any
finite-dimensional space.
The first of these results is apparent by considering, for instance, the <color=#3366CC>tangent</color> function, which provides a <color=#3366CC>one-to-one</color>
<color=#3366CC>correspondence</color> between the <color=#3366CC>interval</color> (/2, /2) andR.The second result was proved by Cantor in 1878, but only became
intuitively apparent in 1890, when <color=#3366CC>Giuseppe Peano</color> introduced the space-filling curves, curved lines that twist and turn
enough to fill the whole of any square, or <color=#3366CC>cube</color>, or hypercube, or finite-dimensional space. These curves can be used to
define a one-to-one correspondence between the points on one side of a square and the points in the square.
Geometry
Until the end of the 19th century, infinity was rarely discussed in <color=#3366CC>geometry</color>, except in the context of processes that
could be continued without any limit. For example, a <color=#3366CC>line</color> was what is now called a line segment, with the proviso that
one can extend it as far as one wants; but extending it infinitely was out of the question. Similarly, a line was usually not
considered to be composed of infinitely many points but was a location where a point may be placed. Even if there are
infinitely many possible positions, only a finite number of points could be placed on a line. A witness of this is the
expression "the <color=#3366CC>locus</color> of a point that satisfies some property" (singular), where modern mathematicians would generally
say "the set of the points that have the property" (plural).
One of the rare exceptions of a mathematical concept involving actual infinity was <color=#3366CC>projective geometry</color>, where points at
infinity are added to the <color=#3366CC>Euclidean space</color> for modeling the <color=#3366CC>perspective</color> effect that shows <color=#3366CC>parallel lines</color> intersecting "at
infinity". Mathematically, points at infinity have the advantage of allowing one to not consider some special cases. For
example, in a <color=#3366CC>projective plane</color>, two distinct <color=#3366CC>lines</color> intersect in exactly one point, whereas without points at infinity, there
are no intersection points for parallel lines. So, parallel and non-parallel lines must be studied separately in classical
geometry, while they need not be distinguished in projective geometry.
Before the use of <color=#3366CC>set theory</color> for the <color=#3366CC>foundation of mathematics</color>, points and lines were viewed as distinct entities, and a
point could be located on a line. With the universal use of set theory in mathematics, the point of view has dramatically
changed: a line is now considered as the set of its points, and one says that a point belongs to a line instead of is
located on a line (however, the latter phrase is still used).
In particular, in modern mathematics, lines are infinite sets.
Infinite dimension
The <color=#3366CC>vector spaces</color> that occur in classical <color=#3366CC>geometry</color> have always a finite dimension, generally two or three. However,
this is not implied by the abstract definition of a vector space, and vector spaces of infinite dimension can be
considered. This is typically the case in <color=#3366CC>functional analysis</color> where function spaces are generally vector spaces of infinite
dimension.
In topology, some constructions can generate <color=#3366CC>topological spaces</color> of infinite dimension. In particular, this is the case of
iterated loop spaces.
Fractals
The structure of a <color=#3366CC>fractal</color> object is reiterated in its magnifications. Fractals can be magnified indefinitely without losing
their structure and becoming "smooth"; they have infinite perimeters and can have infinite or finite areas. One such
fractal curve with an infinite perimeter and finite area is the <color=#3366CC>Koch snowflake</color>.
Finitism
<color=#3366CC>Leopold Kronecker</color> was skeptical of the notion of infinity and how his fellow mathematicians were using it in the 1870s
and 1880s. This skepticism was developed in the <color=#3366CC>philosophy of mathematics</color> called finitism, an extreme form of
mathematical philosophy in the general philosophical and mathematical schools of constructivism and intuitionism.
Logic
In <color=#3366CC>logic</color>, an <color=#3366CC>infinite regress</color> argument is "a distinctively philosophical kind of argument purporting to show that a thesis is
defective because it generates an infinite series when either (form A) no such series exists or (form B) were it to exist,
the thesis would lack the role (e.g., of justification) that it is supposed to play."
In <color=#3366CC>first-order logic</color>, both the <color=#3366CC>compactness theorem</color> and <color=#3366CC>Löwenheim–Skolem theorems</color> are used to construct
non-standard models with certain infinite properties.
Applications
Physics
In <color=#3366CC>physics</color>, approximations of <color=#3366CC>real numbers</color> are used for continuous measurements and <color=#3366CC>natural numbers</color> are used for
discrete measurements (i.e., counting). Concepts of infinite things such as an infinite <color=#3366CC>plane wave</color> exist, but there are no
experimental means to generate them.
Cosmology
The first published proposal that the universe is infinite came from Thomas Digges in 1576. Eight years later, in 1584,
the Italian philosopher and astronomer <color=#3366CC>Giordano Bruno</color> proposed an unbounded universe in On the Infinite Universe
and Worlds: "Innumerable suns exist; innumerable earths revolve around these suns in a manner similar to the way the
seven planets revolve around our sun. Living beings inhabit these worlds."
<color=#3366CC>Cosmologists</color> have long sought to discover whether infinity exists in our physical <color=#3366CC>universe</color>: Are there an infinite number
of stars? Does the universe have infinite volume? Does space "<color=#3366CC>go on forever</color>"? This is still an open question of
<color=#3366CC>cosmology</color>. The question of being infinite is logically separate from the question of having boundaries. The
two-dimensional surface of the Earth, for example, is finite, yet has no edge. By travelling in a straight line with respect
to the Earth's curvature, one will eventually return to the exact spot one started from. The universe, at least in principle,
might have a similar <color=#3366CC>topology</color>. If so, one might eventually return to one's starting point after travelling in a straight line
through the universe for long enough.
The curvature of the universe can be measured through <color=#3366CC>multipole moments</color> in the spectrum of the <color=#3366CC>cosmic background</color>
<color=#3366CC>radiation</color>. To date, analysis of the radiation patterns recorded by the <color=#3366CC>WMAP</color> spacecraft hints that the universe has a flat
topology. This would be consistent with an infinite physical universe.
However, the universe could be finite, even if its curvature is flat. An easy way to understand this is to consider
two-dimensional examples, such as video games where items that leave one edge of the screen reappear on the other.
The topology of such games is <color=#3366CC>toroidal</color> and the geometry is flat. Many possible bounded, flat possibilities also exist for
three-dimensional space.
The concept of infinity also extends to the <color=#3366CC>multiverse</color> hypothesis, which, when explained by astrophysicists such as
<color=#3366CC>Michio Kaku</color>, posits that there are an infinite number and variety of universes. Also, <color=#3366CC>cyclic models</color> posit an infinite
amount of <color=#3366CC>Big Bangs</color>, resulting in an infinite variety of universes after each Big Bang event in an infinite cycle.
Computing
The IEEE floating-point standard (IEEE 754) specifies a positive and a negative infinity value (and also indefinite
values). These are defined as the result of arithmetic overflow, <color=#3366CC>division by zero</color>, and other exceptional operations.
Some <color=#3366CC>programming languages</color>, such as <color=#3366CC>Java</color> and J, allow the programmer an explicit access to the positive and
negative infinity values as language constants. These can be used as <color=#3366CC>greatest and least elements</color>, as they compare
(respectively) greater than or less than all other values. They have uses as sentinel values in <color=#3366CC>algorithms</color> involving
sorting, <color=#3366CC>searching</color>, or windowing.
In languages that do not have greatest and least elements but do allow <color=#3366CC>overloading</color> of relational operators, it is possible
for a programmer to create the greatest and least elements. In languages that do not provide explicit access to such
values from the initial state of the program but do implement the floating-point <color=#3366CC>data type</color>, the infinity values may still be
accessible and usable as the result of certain operations.
In programming, an infinite loop is a loop whose exit condition is never satisfied, thus executing indefinitely.
Arts, games, and cognitive sciences
<color=#3366CC>Perspective</color> artwork uses the concept of vanishing points, roughly corresponding to mathematical points at infinity,
located at an infinite distance from the observer. This allows artists to create paintings that realistically render space,
distances, and forms. Artist <color=#3366CC>M.C. Escher</color> is specifically known for employing the concept of infinity in his work in this
and other ways.
Variations of <color=#3366CC>chess</color> played on an unbounded board are called infinite chess.
<color=#3366CC>Cognitive scientist</color> <color=#3366CC>George Lakoff</color> considers the concept of infinity in mathematics and the sciences as a metaphor. This
perspective is based on the basic metaphor of infinity (BMI), defined as the ever-increasing sequence ‹1, 2, 3, …›.
Primate city

A primate city is a <color=#3366CC>city</color> that is the largest in its <color=#3366CC>country</color>, <color=#3366CC>province</color>, <color=#3366CC>state</color>, or <color=#3366CC>region</color>, and disproportionately larger than any
others in the urban hierarchy. A primate city distribution is a rank-size distribution that has one very large city with many
much smaller cities and <color=#3366CC>towns</color> and no intermediate-sized urban centers, creating a statistical king effect.
The law of the primate city was first proposed by the <color=#3366CC>geographer</color> Mark Jefferson in 1939. He defines a primate city as
being "at least twice as large as the next largest city and more than twice as significant." Aside from size and
population, a primate city will usually have precedence in all other aspects of its country's society such as economics,
politics, culture, and education. Primate cities also serve as targets for the majority of a country or region's internal
migration.
In <color=#3366CC>geography</color>, the phenomenon of excessive concentration of population and development of the main city of a country
or a region (often to the detriment of other areas) is called urban primacy or urban macrocephaly.
Measurement
Urban primacy can be measured as the share of a country's population that lives in the primate city. Relative primacy
indicates the ratio of the primate city's population to that of the second largest in a country or region.
Significance
There is debate as to whether a primate city serves a parasitic or generative function. The presence of a primate city in
a country may indicate an imbalance in development—usually a progressive core and a lagging periphery—on which
the city depends for labor and other resources. However, the urban structure is not directly dependent on a country's
level of economic development.
Many primate cities gain an increasing share of their country's population. This can be due to a reduction in <color=#3366CC>blue-collar</color>
population in the hinterlands because of mechanization and automation. Simultaneously, the number of educated
employees in <color=#3366CC>white-collar</color> endeavors such as politics, finance, media, and higher education rises. These sectors are
clustered predominantly in primate cities where power and wealth are concentrated.
Examples
Some <color=#3366CC>global cities</color> are considered national or regional primate cities. An example of a global city that is also a primate
city is <color=#3366CC>Istanbul</color> in <color=#3366CC>Turkey</color>. Istanbul serves as the primate city of Turkey due to the unmatched economic, cultural, and
educational influence that the city possesses in comparison to other Turkish cities such as the capital <color=#3366CC>Ankara</color>, <color=#3366CC>İzmir</color>, or

<color=#3366CC>Bursa</color>. Likewise, <color=#3366CC>Nairobi</color>, <color=#3366CC>Bangkok</color>, <color=#3366CC>Mexico City</color>, <color=#3366CC>Paris</color>, <color=#3366CC>Cairo</color>, <color=#3366CC>Jakarta</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Seoul</color> have also been described as primate
cities of their respective countries. However, not all regions and countries possess a primate city. The <color=#3366CC>United States</color>
has never had a primate city on a national level due to the <color=#3366CC>decentralized</color> nature of the country and because the
country's second-largest city, <color=#3366CC>Los Angeles</color>, is not far behind the country's largest city, <color=#3366CC>New York City</color>, in either
population or <color=#3366CC>GDP</color>. The <color=#3366CC>metropolitan area</color> of New York City has over 19 million residents, while Los Angeles's has
roughly 13 million residents, as of 2022.
<color=#3366CC>Sub-national divisions</color> can also have primate cities. For instance, New York City is the <color=#3366CC>State of New York</color>'s primate city,
because its population is 32 times bigger than the state's second-largest city of <color=#3366CC>Buffalo</color>. New York City has 44% of the
population and 65% of the GDP of the State of New York. The city of <color=#3366CC>Anchorage</color> is another U.S. example, with around
40% of the total population of <color=#3366CC>Alaska</color> living within the city's limits. <color=#3366CC>China</color> does not have a primate city at a national level,
but several provincial capitals are disproportionately larger than other urban areas in the respective provinces. For

example, <color=#3366CC>Henan</color>, <color=#3366CC>Hubei</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Sichuan</color> have provincial capitals (<color=#3366CC>Zhengzhou</color>, <color=#3366CC>Wuhan</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Chengdu</color>, respectively) that
are significantly larger than the second-largest cities in those provinces, and each of those provinces has a population
similar to that of a large European country. <color=#3366CC>Spain</color> does not have a primate city at the national level because, although
<color=#3366CC>Madrid</color> is the capital and the principal centre of Castilian culture, it is not overwhelmingly larger than <color=#3366CC>Barcelona</color> in either
population or economic importance. Barcelona is also a major cultural centre in its own right as the capital of <color=#3366CC>Catalonia</color>
and the historic centre of Catalan culture. However, the <color=#3366CC>autonomous community</color> of Catalonia has a clear primate city in
Barcelona. Barcelona is several times larger than Catalonia's other major cities (excluding those within its own
metropolitan area), such as Tarragona, Reus, Lleida and Girona, and functions as the region's dominant political,
economic and cultural centre. It contains roughly one-fifth of Catalonia's population, while the Barcelona metropolitan
area is home to over 40% of the autonomous community's residents. <color=#3366CC>India</color> does not have a primate city, as <color=#3366CC>Delhi</color> is not

much larger than <color=#3366CC>Mumbai</color> or <color=#3366CC>Kolkata</color> in terms of population. However, many Indian states, such as <color=#3366CC>Karnataka</color>, <color=#3366CC>West</color>

<color=#3366CC>Bengal</color>, <color=#3366CC>Tamil Nadu</color> and <color=#3366CC>Telangana</color>, do have primate cities: <color=#3366CC>Bangalore</color>, <color=#3366CC>Kolkata</color>, <color=#3366CC>Chennai</color>, <color=#3366CC>Hyderabad</color>, respectively.
Other Indian states, such as <color=#3366CC>Uttar Pradesh</color> and <color=#3366CC>Kerala</color>, do not have any primate cities.
<color=#3366CC>Bangkok</color>, the capital of <color=#3366CC>Thailand</color>, has been called "the most primate city on Earth": in 2000 it was 40 times larger than
the second-largest city of that time, <color=#3366CC>Nakhon Ratchasima</color>. As of 2022, Bangkok is nearly nine times larger than
Thailand's current second-largest city of <color=#3366CC>Chiang Mai</color>, which has been growing in population and has also had its
boundaries expanded to reflect that growth. Taking the concept from his examination of the primate city during the
2010 Thai political protests and applying it to the role that primate cities play if they are national capitals, researcher
Jack Fong noted that when primate cities like Bangkok function as national capitals, they are inherently vulnerable to
insurrection by the military and the dispossessed. He cites the fact that most primate cities serving as national capitals
contain major headquarters for the country. Thus, logistically, it is rather "efficient" to target a national capital that is
also a primate city; most of the governing power is contained in that one small area, and so are most of the people.
The metropolitan area of the city of <color=#3366CC>Moscow</color>, the capital of <color=#3366CC>Russia</color>, is 2.3 times the size of the metropolitan area of the
next largest city, Saint Petersburg, and plays a dominant role as the cultural and political center of the country. It can
therefore be considered a primate city.
Primate cities need not be capital cities: governments may establish a new capital city in an attempt to challenge the
primacy of the largest city or provide more balanced growth. For example, in <color=#3366CC>Tanzania</color>, <color=#3366CC>Dar es Salaam</color> is still the
primate city even though the capital was moved to <color=#3366CC>Dodoma</color>, a new city built to a plan, in 1996. A similar process
(though without building a planned city) occurred when the existing city of <color=#3366CC>Wellington</color> was chosen as <color=#3366CC>New Zealand</color>'s
capital in 1865; <color=#3366CC>Auckland</color>, the capital before the relocation, commanded (and still commands) a greater share of the
population and economy.

For the <color=#3366CC>Philippines</color>, figures are for <color=#3366CC>Metro Manila</color> and Metro Cebu. <color=#3366CC>Manila</color> is the national capital, which is within <color=#3366CC>Metro</color>
<color=#3366CC>Manila</color>, a region. Meanwhile, <color=#3366CC>Cebu City</color> is the capital city of the province of <color=#3366CC>Cebu</color>, with Metro Cebu being its main urban

The list contains 26 countries. If excluding the microstates (which are not listed here and often have one city only) and

In <color=#3366CC>Germany</color>, <color=#3366CC>Munich</color> (city proper population of ca 1.5 million, with surrounding Landkreise ~3 million) is the primate city

people, metro area ~1.35 million). Likewise, in <color=#3366CC>Hesse</color>, <color=#3366CC>Frankfurt</color> (~750,000 people) is nearly three times larger than the

Alessandria; in <color=#3366CC>Campania</color>, <color=#3366CC>Naples</color> has 7 times the population of second-largest <color=#3366CC>Salerno</color> and in <color=#3366CC>Liguria</color>, <color=#3366CC>Genoa</color> at

In <color=#3366CC>Portugal</color>, the Lisbon Metropolitan Area has around 2.8 million people while the Porto Metropolitan Area, the

have around 40% the country's population and are multiple times larger than the third-biggest city, <color=#3366CC>Braga</color>.
North and Central America
In the <color=#3366CC>United States</color>, many primate cities exist at the state level. In <color=#3366CC>California</color>, the population of <color=#3366CC>Los Angeles</color> (~4 million)
is nearly three times that of the second-largest city in the state, <color=#3366CC>San Diego</color>. Likewise, in <color=#3366CC>Illinois</color>, <color=#3366CC>Chicago</color> has 15 times
the population of the state's second-largest city, Aurora, which itself is a suburb of Chicago, and 18 times the
population of Rockford, the state's fifth-largest city and the largest outside of the Chicago metropolitan area, which
comprises nearly two-thirds of the state's population. In <color=#3366CC>New York</color>, <color=#3366CC>New York City</color>, with a 2022 population of about 8.3
million, is more than 30 times larger than the state's second-largest city of <color=#3366CC>Buffalo</color>. Erie County, where Buffalo is
located, is the eighth-largest county in the state and the largest outside of the New York metropolitan area, with around
950,000 residents; on the other hand, New York City alone contains four of the six largest counties in the state, each
with at least 1.35 million residents.

Canada also has several primate cities at the provincial level: <color=#3366CC>Vancouver</color> for <color=#3366CC>British Columbia</color>; <color=#3366CC>Winnipeg</color> for <color=#3366CC>Manitoba</color>;

<color=#3366CC>Toronto</color> for <color=#3366CC>Ontario</color>; <color=#3366CC>Montreal</color> for <color=#3366CC>Quebec</color>; <color=#3366CC>Halifax</color> for <color=#3366CC>Nova Scotia</color>; and <color=#3366CC>St. John's</color> for <color=#3366CC>Newfoundland and Labrador</color>.
Oceania
<color=#3366CC>Australia</color> does not have a primate city, but at the state level, each of the capital cities of the states and territories act as
the primate city of that state or territory.
